title: Senate Moves Closer to Changing College Sports Forever
summary:
College sports are huge in America. Players score touchdowns and hit three-pointers in front of thousands of fans. But did you know that until recently, many college athletes couldn't make money from their own names? That's changing — and now the U.S. Senate is trying to make new rules.

This week, senators voted 74-24 to close debate on a bill called the Protect College Sports Act. That means they're closer to a final vote. If it passes the Senate, it goes to the House of Representatives.

So what would the bill do? First, it would make official the revenue sharing deal that lets schools share up to 22% of certain money with athletes. This year, that's $21.58 million per school. It also adds a $27.5 million "retention pool" to keep players on the team. That could reduce how much money players get from third-party name, image, and likeness (NIL) deals — like when a player is paid to appear in a commercial.

The bill would also limit athletes to one "free" transfer without having to sit out a season. It would stop coaches from leaving one school for another during the season. And it would give the NCAA (the group that makes college sports rules) some protection from lawsuits.

Not everyone agrees. The powerful Southeastern and Big Ten conferences don't like a part that would let conferences pool their media rights. They say it wouldn't make more money. The bill also says conferences can't grow beyond 19 teams. It's a big change for a multibillion-dollar industry.
why_it_matters: Lots of kids play school sports and dream of playing in college, and these rules decide whether college athletes can be paid, how often they can switch schools, and what the games we watch will look like in a few years.

background_read: The Senate is one of the two parts of the U.S. Congress (the group that makes the country's laws), and it has 100 members — two from each state.

For many years, college athletes were not allowed to earn money from their fame; then, after a court case in 2021, the NCAA — the National Collegiate Athletic Association (the group that makes rules for college sports) — allowed name, image, and likeness deals.
If the bill passes the Senate, it still has to pass the House of Representatives (the other part of Congress) before it can become a law.
Article_Structure: WHO: U.S. senators, college athletes, the NCAA, and the Southeastern and Big Ten conferences.
WHAT: Senators voted 74-24 to close debate on the Protect College Sports Act, moving it closer to a final vote.
WHERE: The U.S. Senate first, and then the House of Representatives if it passes.
WHY: The bill would make revenue sharing official, add a retention pool, limit athletes to one free transfer, and give the NCAA protection from lawsuits.

perspectives.description: Athletes can already earn money from their own names, and the bill would make schools' revenue sharing official — but the retention pool might reduce some of their outside deals.
The Southeastern and Big Ten conferences don't like the part that lets conferences pool media rights, and they may also dislike limits on how big a conference can grow.
The NCAA would get protection from lawsuits, which it wants, but the bill also makes new national rules that every school would have to follow.
